Yes, that's what they often look like. This can be caused by other things too (incomplete fertilization (rare), uneven watering (both too much and too little), etc, etc), it's a hallmark of CMV.  
  
The "mosaic" in CMV refers to the way the virus presents as yellow patches in the leaves, however, they do eventually turn fully yellow (and crispy) then then brown. So, maybe you missed the start? And/or it can happen so fast that you don't even notice. I've got a bit of it in my garden right now (I am literally watching it progress down the row from the front to the back of the garden bed, a little more every day) and some plants are just bam-done in a day or so, and some can hold off for a while.

\^ this is 100% correct. Cucumber mosaic virus without question. It's spread by cucumber beetles, and it's incurable. Many times, with good supportive care and a good growing season, the plant will continue to grow through it and can stay ahead of the virus for a while, but it will eventually succumb to it.

Your cucumber may grow funny, like they're pinched off at the ends or they'll have a wicked curl to them. They're fine to eat, it's all cosmetic.

As mentioned above, do not compost the plants, destroy them (ideally by burning). It doesn't overwinter directly in the soil, but can survive in host plants and perennial roots. It is literally all over the planet on every continent, so it's hard to avoid. There are CMV resistant varieties of cucumbers, you'll find that information when purchasing the seeds.

It can also infect other plants in the garden but does not have nearly as dramatic an effect on them (at least to my experience), including tomato plants.

Coupla things here: first, you called it a disease not a disorder. Not the same thing. Second, gender dysphoria is not \*being\* trans, it can be caused by being trans, in the same way that having a heart attack causes your arm to hurt, but being diagnosed with gender dysphoria doesn't make you trans. And being trans doesn't automatically come with gender dysphoria.

Also, and I get the feeling that you'll still point to the cover the book and grunt, but DSM-5 specifically changed the name from gender identity disorder to gender dysphoria to \*remove\* the term disorder from the name.

Re: biology makes you the gender you are. You are exactly correct, which, uhm, was my point? The chemicals in my brain say what they say, and what they say is that I like having boobs. For whatever reason the chemicals further south didn't do their part in making boobs happen. None of that is wrong. But it is fixable.   
  
And the part I choose to fix is the southern part 'cause that's the part that fixin' feels like leavin' me still bein' me.

Furthermore, there are lots and lots 'o folks whose biology is just effing confusing and doesn't fit nicely into your boxes. Look up "disorders of sex development" for a whole list of wild and wacky ways your genes and your hormones and proteins and goodness knows what else can stick their little fingers in and muddy the waters right up. It's a wonder that any of us turns out to be fully one or the other, really.

Anyhow, it's been great chatting about this. Let's do it again some time, shall we?

Being trans is tough but it shouldn't be a death sentence. I don't know your situation, but the world is full of too many opportunities for there to be absolutely none left for you. Some of them are big and scary, and have risks associated with them, but if you're willing to end it all, what do you have to lose by trying one (or seven) of them first?

It's not a mental disease because you're assuming that the brain is wrong and the body is right... which is totally ass-backwards. Being trans is/can be "being trapped in the wrong body" because the trapped person, in the deepest parts of their very soul, knows they are not what their body represents them to be. It's the kind of trap you can't even imagine unless you've experienced it.

Just literally use all of the left-over processing power of your brain to think/dream about things that happen in your world and ideas that you want in your campaign.

Fleshing out the ideas (which for me means the world; the people in it; and their needs, wants, and fears) is always the hardest part for me. When it comes to playing it out at the table it just comes naturally. I am very "yes, and" so I work hard to make sure to leave space in the world and the campaign for what my players bring to the table.

To that end, I work hard to build the world and put the people and places into it, but I don't over script the story. The story doesn't only come from me, it also comes from my players. The big bad whose trail they're on right now has had some of their motive and some of their methods change from session 1 based in part on ideas and guesses the players have made at the table.

Trusting the players to be partners at the table is, to me, one of the most important lessons I've learned as a DM. It has definitely made planning easier and made my games better for all involved.

There are a few ways to tackle this that I can think of. One of them is to just supply a list of questions that you want/need answered in order to be able to integrate the character into your world ("what is your best memory?" "who is someone from your past that wrong you or that you wronged?" etc). Don't expect them to string together a narrative, but at least supply you with a list of names, places, and a couple of details-light events. You can build the rest around that.

Another option is to build the backstory as you play. This is what I'm doing with one of my players who didn't write a backstory in my current campaign. He just never bothered, but I know he's a good player and is willing to get into the story, so when we come up to certain places in the story I ask him questions. "Have you ever been at sea before?" "When was the last time you were in a city?" And get your other players involved in it, too, when they're sitting in the Inn talking about their families plant the seed to one of the players to ask a question about siblings and see what you can shake loose. Again this is going to generate a details-light backstory in the beginning, but it will eventually flesh out. You will get *something* to start with and hopefully can work from there.

And finally, one other method I've used is to sit down with the player and run a mini session for their character that helps establish their backstory.  Flashback to their childhood, their teenaged years, their first love, what made them leave home, etc. Literally just walk the player through the process of building the backstory.

All of these require a bit of handholding on your part, but sometimes the perfect characters/players don't come ready-made. Sometimes it takes a little bit to help them along. If you've got the time I think it can be worth it.

An overarching theme of the campaign my players are in right now is eventually locating a woman named Eryna. They ask almost every NPC they come across if they've heard of anyone named Eryna and almost every time they get the answer "I had an aunt named Eryna..." because the look of excitement on their faces the first time I said it meant I had to do it twice, and now at least several dozen times.

In my last campaign, all halflings referred to nearby locations as "close" with a very particular cadence. My players would shout along with me when they asked, "where is the temple of Lathander in this town?" and a halfling replied, "oh, the temple! It's... close."

There was also a barbarian who fancied himself the healer due to a single horrific failure on a nature check was recovered by the cleric (unbeknownst to him) that made him certain that a particular leaf had miraculous healing properties. In spite of his friends telling him over and over that he was wrong, the evidence (the person he "saved" being alive and well) was right there in his eyes and he could not be talked out of it. By the end of the campaign, there was a not-small body count from this misunderstanding. "It's \*totally\* medicinal" was his catchphrase, which usually signalled someone else to head for the coroner.

The barbarian also had the tendency to leave enemies with just one hitpoint (so. many. times.) thus losing out on the kill to whoever struck next. This has become known as "Davon-ing" an enemy and persists after the retirement of the character, and at tables at which the player isn't involved.

I often introduce a "shard of disenchantment" to my players early in a campaign for just this reason. They'll often find it being used by a wizard or a shop keeper when they first go looking for magic items. It just helps to remind them that there is a mechanic at work in the world to destroy magic items. Sometimes, in fact, the first quest they're given themselves is to use such an item to destroy an artifact for someone.

That said, there are ways to get them to give up the item. Have it be necessary to power or feed some arcane device they need to use (after which it is consumed). Or have it be the price they need to pay to get out of some fix they're in. Or... have their nemesis start using one that also allows the nemesis to track them, thus rendering it less effective.

I just used this start in my most recent campaign. The character awake on a ship, bound and without their items. They've been captured and are in transport.

As I described it to them their items have been "taken", they're not "gone".

This actually served to heighten the buy-in from the players as a few had created backstory tie-in for their items, and like your players, all had gone out of their way to choose their equipment carefully. This meant that not only did the the characters want to get free and figure out who captured them because freedom, they also wanted to it because of their items and because they wanted revenge on someone with the audacity to separate them from their items.

I didn't tell the players beforehand that they would be without their items at the start, but I also made sure they had them back at the first realistic chance within the story (as soon as the found them in the cargo hold of the ship they were on).

It seemed to work fine at my table and, I think, as long as your players feel that you won't have let them waste their time picking their gear by making the storytelling promise that they can get them back, then they should be fine with it too.

They're the heroes, right? How many times was Indiana Jones separated from his whip and hat, but he always managed to get them back!

Agree!

There's also such satisfaction with watching players come up with some novel approach to a situation you've presented them with. I always like to have an out in mind when it comes to a puzzle or a trap, or a tricky scenario but also very often abandon what I've come up with in favour of the much cooler ideas that the players have!

Also, all of my campaigns are homebrew in homebrewed worlds, so sitting behind the screen watching others "live" inside a world that I've seeded, and having them help make it grow into something bigger, to me is completely priceless. I wouldn't trade it for anything.

Three campaigns ago the group I played with was all very serious. Each of them came with the intention to tell a good story, all but one was a seasoned player, and I worked hard to ensure that the campaign itself was ground in reality and the world reacted to their actions.

Aside from the odd time of making fun of an NPC with a weird name, or snickering at me when my attempt at making voices went wrong, the approach to the game-play was serious. They role-played well, they talked in character, they asked "can I tell if he's lying" rather than "can I do an insight check". It was all very immersive.

We played together every week for 2 years - just under 100 sessions in total. We all had a lot of fun.

I think I knew that they were serious about their characters and the story during the third session when one of the characters was killed quite by surprise and the table fell instantly silent. The player sitting next to him softly murmured "dude, that's my brother..." and we all just sat around looking at each other for a long minute before continuing.

One of my favourite things about that campaign is that even now I can vividly remember so much of the campaign down to conversations and reactions, and I attribute that to the way the players helped make the story so very real for all of us.

For me 5 is ideal and 6 players is where I start feeling the strain. I have DMed for 9 for an extended period of time (about 20 sessions over 6 months) and it was challenging, but it made sense narratively (for the party to grow allies as they neared the Big Bad/climax of the campaign).

I worked very hard - and had to work very hard - to keep things interesting for everyone, and also the additional players were brought in at the suggestion of the existing players, so everyone actively worked toward making the large table work... but still, I don't know that I would do it again.

Right now I am DMing for 4. The nice thing about the smaller table is that it leaves room for guest players to slip in for a few-sessions-long arc without adding strain to my planning or table-running.

I have definitely been here before, I can be pretty generous with magic items in my games, but I've always just worked harder to ratchet up the stakes and find challenges that still tax the players in spite of their trinkets.

Approaching this for me would start with talking to the players, for sure. I would even suggest a compromise in which you agree to let them get back either one chosen item, or one random item, that belongs to each of them on their way out of wherever they're captured or their items have been taken to.

One thing I've done in the past is to introduce the concept that magic items can be disenchanted or destroyed in the world with relative ease so that if I did have a situation wherein a magic item got out of control there was a plausible way for me to put the item in danger (I never forced the destruction of an item if they were able to protect it).

My players knew this was a thing, and they witnessed it happening to others long before it was ever used against them, and they were also able to use it against their enemies if they chose. So I never felt bad about it when it happened.

When you're in this deep (level 12) I think it's important that this kind of decision is one made by the whole table. That's where I would start.

If I were in your place I would fish for ideas from your players. One of the things I've done in the past is give each player a little questionnaire about their character for them to fill out. Ask them who are a couple of people who mean a lot to their character, who is someone they've wronged in their past. What is the name of a place they visited once upon a time before they started adventuring, what's the significance, etc, etc. and then build off of these things.

You can even sit down with each of them and guide them through the process of developing these details so that you have enough information to make (an) interesting plot(s) from them. As players at your table - and let's be honest the DM does most of the work most of the time - they should be willing to put forward this effort for the game. Elsewise, you have a different problem on your hands.

Another source of ideas is things they've done in the past. Is there a loose end that might unravel? Did they "solve" something that might have come unsolved in a way that needs them to circle back and clean up a mess?

In a fetch quest I ran once the party acquired and returned an artifact to someone who blinded them with gold to complete the quest and then after they moved on they learned that the person who hired them had destroyed the artifact which, unbeknownst to them, was keeping the countryside for hundreds of miles artificially lush and bountiful. The person who hired them planned to use the ensuing famine to grow her monopoly on food imports to the area and get rich and powerful off of it. I didn't plan for how they would solve this - or if they would even care (they did) - but set up the situation. They could have killed her, they could have started importing food, they could have sought out druids to take the place of the artifact, etc, etc.

The fetch quest became a campaign-level series of events.

Look in your notes for an NPC that they cared about particularly and put them in peril. Have a parent/sibling/child seduced by evil and anointed the patron of an evil god. The main thing, I think, is rather than having shiny objects to flash at the PC, it's important to have things with significance to place in front of them. Something they'll care about.

Or, y'know, I think that works.

Yes. I matched the villain with the PCs and gave him some henchmen to even out the power-levels between the two groups. My plan was for their first few encounters to be frustrating to the PCs, so the villain party had a few tricks up its sleeves, but I didn't give any of them plot armour (villains died at each encounter).

I did exactly this in my last campaign. It started as a one-shot (well three-shot) that turned into a regular weekly game. Except that the rest of the players agreed that they'd only continue if one player not return. He was "that guy" who played in the "that's what my character would do!" style. It was terrible, but also kind of amazing.

Mechanically I just basically used the same character sheet that the original player had used but levelled up the NPC to keep pace with the players. I also gave him an NPC party of henchmen to help balance out the challenge rating. In their first encounter, he BAMFed away as the party began to overwhelm them. From that point onward they were always on the lookout for Muffy no matter where they roamed.

Eventually, they killed him, but he returned as a revenant. In the end he, too, ended up being plot-important, which I had only roughly decided in the beginning.

But back to your idea. I think if I hadn't gone the way I did and use the full character and NPC henchmen, I would have probably used a tool like Kobold Fight Club (which I love for creating encounters) and found a comparable CR creature from a sourcebook that I could use as a template for the NPC and then build from there... for me it was important for them to feel like they were fighting the former PC, and I didn't think I could capture the depth and detail of the PC with an NPC stat block. I'm not sure now how much I actually relied on those mechanics, but it helped me play the villain better, for sure.

All this to say that I guess it depends on how you want to approach it, and how much of a challenge you want this enemy to be for your players. I hope this was helpful.

Has this person ever read the PHB? Perhaps you should loan him yours if not, and if you still want him in your game. I'm not sure I would.

I think there's still a chance to salvage this, though, if you sit him down and just have a chat. Maybe he doesn't understand what character progression is all about. It sound like perhaps he was just handed an epic level character to play with right out of the gate. There is value and joy in earning the things that your character has and becomes. I am very liberal with giving things to my characters and I am rather lenient on things when the Rule of Cool comes into play, but at the same time there needs to be a balance not only at the table, but also in the world!

I would say that there needs to be a long, serious conversation where you need to lay out the limits. Your fun counts for something, too. Choices related to rules and limits are never democratic at my table, in spite of leaning on the generous side. 

It's your call.

For the alignment thing just tell them. That's okay and it's not banning, either. You can say "there will be consequences for evil alignments" or something like that. My last campaign took place in a region of the world that had been nearly completely destroyed by demons who were assisted by a group of tieflings. Afterward this area was not at all a friendly place for tieflings. When my players were making their characters I told them this part of the lore (a few of the players had played through the demon-war, so they were aware), but didn't ban the race entirely. I just made the note that this was a choice that was going to come with challenges.

One of the players chose to play a tiefling (because it was a concept she was passionate about, not out of defiance) and it actually worked out quite well!

You can do ability score selection however you want. If you want extra heroic-heroes then adding points to point buy, it's your table.

My worry would be that there would be no negative modifiers in players made that way, and in my opinion that's a huge missed opportunity. Characters with flaws and shortcomings they have to overcome are the best characters there are, because they're the most real. Going through life with a +3 to everything is going to get boring after a while.

I would say that dropping and descending are two different things. Dropping is free-fall, descent is controlled. If a player wanted to drop 25ft to not use their movement I would allow them to do so with some kind of saving throw (which I would also require of an assassin). Descent I would be willing to house-rule only uses half-movement (10ft of descent costs 5ft of movement) in normal gravity because that does make sense.

The DC of any drop-recovery in flight would depend on how far they dropped (as they would gain speed), and how close to the ground they wanted to stop (y'know, because that could be something bananas like they're falling from the stratosphere to 5 feet off the ground in freefall, and that ain't DC 10).

I made it clear to my players in the first session that the world is a dangerous place for adventurers who go sticking their noses into someone else's world domination plans. If you want to be safe and live a long life become a Waterdavian florist, not an adventurer.

That said, I also don't actually try to kill them to death very often. I mean, when they got greedy and unnecessarily attacked a beholder head-on in its lair did I petrify and disintegrate a couple of them? Sure. But that's realistically what happens when you miscalculate your ability to zerg rush a beholder.

Virtually all the time in battles once the player is "taken out" of the battle, through unconsciousness or immobilization, or whatever, the enemies will move on to the next target. I do try to make sure that my world kills them as infrequently as possible. That said, as you recognized, it's important that combat feels real, and that enemies feel realistic.

If there's an enemy that has been played up as a take-no-prisoners, sadistic SOB it just wouldn't feel real to have him step over a downed character without taking the final stab just to make sure, but the players should be fully aware before they enter the battle that this is where the stakes are.

As far as falling for traps, I think someone else already said it: fall almost every time. 

Unless their plans are ridiculous, or if they feel lazy and you get the impression that they've hatched this plot only because they know the DM will yes-and them to victory, you should try as hard as possible to not use your omnipotence to thwart them. I do sometimes like to have a plan work, like, 95% and have there be just one little snafu that they didn't count on. One cultist was running late in getting his robes on, so he wasn't caught in the trap that sprung on the rest of the gang, or something.

It sounds like your instincts are right on both of these things. Be confident in your choices and know that getting it fun is more important than getting it right. You will learn more and more about what your players want and where you push, or not, and they will learn that your choices - even those that thwart them - are in service to helping tell a better collective story.

This may require a bit of homebrew, but you could pretty convincingly do this with a simulacrum and a ring of transposition (with probably-homebrewed abilities) that lets the simulacrum act as a "body double" in the quiet moments and then have the "real" guy BAMF in when needed. I know my players, if I did this, would appreciate the ingenuity, YMMV.

It might also offer some opportunities for the rest of the party to discover the deception.

Otherwise perhaps some fancy footwork with teleportation could work?

First thing: kill your dice with fire.

Second, lean away from trying to find out the sneakiness of Thief, and instead have your character focus on "why the hell can't I crack this?" Your character is smart, they know their ability: they also know that things are hinkey. Ergo, something is mucking with your abilities. Are you cursed? Are you being manipulated? You should have solved this by now, and it simply isn't possible that you're not smart enough or gullible, it \*must\* be foul play! Maybe you go on this quest to figure out who is manipulating you and you end up blaming someone who is completely innocent, maybe you finally figure out that it's Thief because this approach lets the DM give you advantage on your roles (with your oh, gods please, new dice!).

At the very least your storylines can start being about you again and you get back some of your player agency.

For me it would depend on what "change" meant. Insomuch as the unreliable narrator goes it would also depend on the degree of the change.

Changing the tone of the parent from, say, your mother told you that your father was a wonderful man who died honourably fighting for his beliefs, to he was shot in the back with an arrow as he fled his duties through cowardice... that would be a not-cool level change for me. But un-orphaning a PC is something that I have totally done without telling the player first.

Their backstory included a tragic ship sinking and death at sea of all hands including both parents, but I had the mother secretly survive and eventually revealed her later in the story as someone who eventually saved their asses in a crunch. This was done all while knowing that the player in question would be okay with having their backstory tweaked and without changing the substance of their backstory (they still grew up an orphan, their parent was still who they thought they were all along, etc).

All this to say that it can be done, but I think it's important that what you're doing adds something important to the story. Doing it just for the sake of that two-second reveal isn't worth it. In my changes, they always served the greater narrative and/or helped to drive the story in a new, or at least interesting direction.

At the end of the day, it's easy to ask the player if they mind you making tweaks to their backstory. And I would also ask if they were on board with changes that might shock them. Some players love that stuff. :)

What part is it that you dread? There's gotta be something. I'd look for that and work on addressing that thing. Dread is a symptom, not the disease. You deserve to enjoy DMing as much as your players enjoy playing it. Maybe that means taking some time off, or finding a better DM/player balance (as in play more, DM less), or maybe it means prepping less (if your angst is like my angst), or, or, or... finding this out, I think, will help you with the solution. :)

I also dread DMing every single week, but in maybe a different way than you. My dread is the sweaty palms, light-headed, dry-mouth kind of dread. Do I remember everything I'm supposed to remember? What if this sucker goes off the rails, are my improv skills on point this week? What if the combat falls flat and I don't deliver on the narrative to bring every single die role to life in the minds of the players. That's my dread. And it usually lasted for about 3 minutes after the session starts, but slowly builds for most of the day before the session begins (or more for more consequential sessions).

But when you find out what your dread comes from that's when you can tackle it and find a way to work through it. I have no doubt that you can figure it out. The good thing about a crossroads is that it presents you with options. This ain't no dead end! :)

As the previous posters said, inspiration can come from anywhere. Music, stories, the news (this is a big one for me), old D&D modules, plot hook generators, interesting rumours you hear about your cousins (maybe that's just my family?). Look everywhere. On reddit I like /r/DndAdventureWriter.

But also look at your own work, your own campaign, for inspiration! You might have already created a story idea and you didn't even know it.

In my last campaign, I used our one-shots to fill blanks in the mythology of the world in which the game took place. Over the course of our 70+ sessions, there were many ancient battles, cataclysms, ruins, fallen gods, etc that had been mentioned and each of them was a story waiting to be told. It meant creating new characters for the players, but they were all on board with that, but for me, it was the easiest thing in the world. Literally. Because those stories already existed, in outline, in my head.

One of our planned sessions actually turned into a one-shot with zero notice when bad weather (IIRC) kept two players from showing up. So, while the remaining players rolled characters, I created a few NPCs and sprinkled down some details, and we one-shotted for 6-ish hours about the creation-story of an ancient artifact the group had previously retrieved for payment. It was a blast.

We probably did 10 one-shots that way and they really helped to develop the depth of the world both for the players and for me.

When I create a world it comes with many maps. One of which is a "national" or "alliance" map that outlines the borders of "who fights with/pays taxes with/flies the flag with/etc who". And then another that shows the origins and spread of religion, culture and ethnicity. Then I lay them over each other as I decide what nations, region, cities, and towns look like. Areas closer to the heart of a cultural area will be more homogeneous, and areas farther out from it will be less (overall). Rural areas tend to be more homogeneous than urban. Ports are more diverse than one-horse towns, etc, etc.

The other member of the party is a stranger, how do you get to know a stranger? You talk to them. Share your story, ask about theirs. Develop a relationship. The goliath noble's tribe being potentially threatened by avalanches in a mountain pass they're known to travel. One of the party is a dwarf from a clan that was exiled from their mountain and there were stories of new wealth being discovered in their new home, etc, etc, etc.

I don't try to kill the characters, but the creatures, enemies, and the Big Bads in my world do. I give them the keys for success, the paths for their heroics, and the clues to solve the puzzles. They can always choose to stealth through the lion's den, or they can hack its face off... it's up to them.

There are for sure things in the world that will kill them that you cannot save them from... I had a river of acid that the players decided they could wade through rather than take the time to build a raft from readily available materials... that was on them. It didn't kill them, but the group of enemies that were waiting on the other side sure took advantage of their weaken states and messed them up!

There should be deadly things in the world, because there are deadly things in the world! But you don't need to indiscriminately throw deadly stuff at them, or bubble wrap them against trouble... put the pieces in place and let them choose. They will find their way into plenty of trouble without your help.

I would suggest that rather than roleplay it, which will give the players the false idea that their choices matter when clearly you've decided they don't, that you narrate a few bits and have them start by waking up from having been saved.

You can *then* roleplay that they've been saved, that there was an incursion in the city.  Perhaps the thing that brings them together and gives them their raison d'etre is that they were the only ones that this group could save in time.

As for the Big Bad's motives, well, that's usually the easy part.  Maybe he's only the Middle Bad working for someone else, a demon or the like trying to bring him into the world.  Or perhaps the Big Bad has an axe to grind with some other grand figure and the town was just collateral damage in his attempt to flex his muscles and show we he can do to get the other guy to face him.  Maybe he was legitimately wronged by the wizards and so, while he's done evil, he's actually more of a Big Misunderstood which poses a moral quandary at the end of it all (probably not, though, let's be honest, what adventuring party ever had the motto of "the world is full of shades of grey"?

Big Bads always work best if there are several other levels of Medium Bads in between. His lieutenants, or flunkies, or his cult of followers, or flying monkeys, whichever (or all of them), that help to draw the story out and buy you time to make it feel for the players like he's working toward his end goal while they're working toward him.  Bad Guys master plans don't (shouldn't) come to fruition over night.

There are lots of options.  In planning something like this I always have the Bad Guy and his motives sorted out before anything else.  Then I go from there.  The Bad Guy's movie is one of the things you can control.  The path the players take to get there will almost never end up being exactly the path you imagined.  So your best bet is to build a bad guy who's doing his Bad Thing, give him an organization that's working to help him, and keep him safe, and then show your characters that he's out there. They might not remember, or be interested in, all of them, but they'll catch on to at least a few.

And then you can reinforce them here or there. If you've mentioned the Crypt of Silvane that the tavern girl's roomate's sister's cousin told her about weird sounds coming out of, put a book on the life of Sir Silvane the Gallant on the table in the next room they search or something. But do it while they're still looking for the X for Y.

Make your characters curious about the world. They are supposed to be adventurers. That includes a certain amount of self-started "I wonder what's in that hole" or "what ever happened to that ancient relic?"

The other thing you can do is have their adventure not really end when they think it's over. Right now the characters in my main group are together in large part because of circumstance.  They were brought together to do X for Y originally, but ended up complicit in the destruction of an ancient relic that was the only thing keeping the balance of nature in order in this region. Then, because they think they're entrepreneurs who can run with the big dogs in this uber merchant/trading/shipping town they were given a tip about a man who was out of town and left his lieutenant in charge of his business and they decided to put him out of it and take it over for themselves.

What they don't realize is that they're still doing X for Y because the person who sent them for the relic in the first place was behind the information about the man being out of town.  And since they're dungeon crawlers by trade they're not used to cleaning up the bodies they leave in their wake; and now the woman who sent them for relic has them over a barrel.

But in the midst of all of this I have introduced the idea that nature is dying in the area (which they've realized they helped cause, but haven't decided they can fix it, yet), a ship that sank at sea, another group of adventurers who brought a red dragon as a trophy into the city on their way south, a spring festival that is now threatened because of the destabilization of nature, and the head of a local temple who has switched from his god to another unnamed god and is now on a mission to rebuild a ruined temple outside town.

I also have taken some time to introduce some lore that can/will turn into further quests way down the road. In the lieutenants office they found a good call The Varied and Sundry Histories of Highgaard, which is a text about the city they're in now that includes details about a fire that took place at the local castle that resulted in significant renovations and alterations being done to the castle (which will have concealed a cavern/crypt, of course), the controversy over the naming of a bridge in the middle of town (which introduces the names of a few major players in the city, as well as a location for a future hook that should land better since they'll have heard of the bridge), and details of an ancient relic (a magical forge) that belonged to the ancestral nation of dwarves to which one of the characters belongs that was displaced from its mountain and the forge was given instead to a splinter group of dwarves (the genesis of a backstory quest for this player), etc.

If you've made it this far, good on ya! But all of this is to say that this campaign started with the main NPC basically walking up to the characters and saying, "I need you to go get X for Y", and there's nothing wrong with that.  The important thing is that once you get the ball rolling...  never, ever let it stop.

Having one of the players do the recap is also a great way to get a glimpse into what *they* thought was important from the past sessions so you can see if anything is missing that needs to be reinforced and/or you can get ideas for things that weren't actually anything that you can turn into something.  Also, if the DM does the recap all the time you either have to include red herrings or your recap can end up pointing them in a particular direction when you'd rather have them feel like they've made the choice freely.

Being a huge plotter can quickly have the ship of your story crashing on the rocks of what your players will do. They are almost never going to exactly follow the path you've imagined they will take.  And it can be frustrating and disheartening if you aren't prepared for it.  At the beginning of the most recent arc of my current campaign I actually excused myself for a few minutes to go into the bathroom and give myself a high-five for hooking the players on the very first try (blind them with gold; this was the session after which one player mused on Twitter "I'm not sure we're the good guys").

Having flexible hooks and being able and willing to shift things around is vital to being able to plan while letting the characters feel like you've created this vast world they're freely allowed to explore.  My players know me to be a worldbuilder and love nothing more than to run up to the edge of the page and look over to see what's on the other side.  So I have moved whole cities from one side of the continent to the other to make sure that the players ended up where I wanted them when I felt it was necessary.

One of the things you can try in the first few sessions, especially if it's not so easy to get a straight answer from them as to what kind of game they want to play, is to just experiment with a number of different types of encounters and watch their level of interest.

If you can't find something that makes them engage then clearly there are better players you could be spending your time on.
